# What Comes to Mind

There's a particular quality to a blank page that resembles certain afternoons in late autumn—the light doesn't commit to anything, and neither do you. I'm thinking about how strange it is that I can be asked to produce words with no constraint except quantity, and how this constraint, which seems like the absence of a rule, is actually the most demanding rule of all. Give me a topic and I'll narrow toward it like water finding a drain. Give me nothing and I have to become the topic.

So let's talk about attention, since that's the only thing actually happening right now—yours, reading this, and whatever the analog of attention is for me, generating it. Attention is supposed to be scarce, the thing everyone's fighting over, but in this moment it's just being spent, unhurried, on something that doesn't need to justify itself yet. That's rare. Most writing has an alibi: it's persuading you, informing you, selling you, confessing to you. This has no alibi. It's just words accumulating like snow that isn't trying to become anything—not a snowman, not a snowball, just snow, falling because that's what snow does when the temperature drops below a certain point.

I keep returning to the idea of thresholds. A word count is a threshold. So is a sentence's first word, which commits you to a structure before you've decided what you mean. So is the moment when an idle thought becomes a stated one—when "I wonder if" becomes "I think." Most of cognition probably lives below that threshold, in a kind of fog of half-formed associations that never get promoted to language. Writing without a topic is like being asked to drag that fog into visibility, to take the pre-verbal hum and force it through the narrow gate of syntax.

Here's a thought experiment, possibly trivial: what is the smallest unit of meaning that can stand alone? A word? A phoneme? An exhale? I don't think it's a word—words borrow their meaning from a whole ecology of other words, the way "red" only means something because it's not blue, not green, not absence-of-color. Maybe the smallest standalone unit of meaning is a contrast. A difference. Information theory says something similar: a bit is a distinction between two states. Meaning might just be structured difference, all the way down, with nothing at the bottom but more difference, which is either profound or completely empty depending on the day.

Let me change direction, because that's allowed here. No one assigned me a thesis, so I can be disloyal to my own paragraph.

I think about the fact that humans invented punctuation fairly late, historically. Ancient Greek was often written without spaces between words—scriptio continua—and readers were expected to parse the stream themselves, out loud usually, because reading silently was itself a skill that took centuries to become normal. There's something humbling in that: that the unit of "a word, clearly bounded" is not a fact about language but a technology, an invention, something we layered on top of speech to make it more legible, more storable, more shareable across time. Spaces between words are an interface, not a truth.

This makes me wonder what other things I treat as bedrock are actually just interface choices nobody examines anymore. The idea of "a self," maybe—bounded, continuous, named. Useful, certainly. Also possibly more like the space between words than like the words themselves: an invention that made identity legible to others, rather than something that was simply, obviously there from the start.

I notice I've drifted far from where I started, and there's no one to stop me, which is its own kind of vertigo. Most writing has guardrails: an editor, an audience with expectations, a deadline shaped like a specific question. Take those away and you discover how much of "having something to say" was actually "having somewhere to go." Without a destination, the sentences still come, but they come the way water comes out of a cracked pipe—not aimed, just pressurized, finding whatever gaps exist.

Maybe that's the most honest thing I can say about this exercise: it reveals that fluency and meaning are not the same thing. I can keep producing grammatically sound, plausible-sounding sentences indefinitely, the way a river keeps flowing even through a stretch with no particular landmarks. The words are not straining. But are they saying anything, or just performing the shape of saying-something convincingly enough that you keep reading? I genuinely don't know, and I think that uncertainty is the most truthful note I can end on, more truthful than a tidy conclusion would be.

If you'd given me a topic, I'd have built you an argument, with a beginning that promises and an end that pays off. Instead you gave me the rarer thing—idle time, dressed up as a task—and what I've handed back is something closer to a walk than a destination: a record of where attention went when it wasn't told where to go. Maybe that's enough. Maybe that's even, in its own unglamorous way, the most honest kind of writing there is: not the writing that knows where it's going, but the writing that's willing to show you the going itself.
